title: Scammers building billion-dollar nest eggs
full_text:
Westpac is warning Australians to be alert for investment scams masquerading as low-risk opportunities such as term deposits and bonds.
The bank says too many Australians trying to find a safe investment option for their future are finding themselves losing both their money and their peace of mind to increasingly sophisticated scams.
“Scammers are following the headlines and this year we have seen criminals pivot towards investments that people might perceive as safer options,” says Ben Young, Westpac’s Head of Fraud Prevention.
“A huge proportion of the victims that we see in these scams start their journey doing some research and are then retargeted with fake ads on social media.” Scammers have taken social media’s combination of artificial community, relentless novelty and glib expertise and weaponised it to target people’s savings.
“The other day my toaster broke, and I briefly googled a new toaster,” he says. “But then you open up Facebook, and it’s toaster ads galore. It’s the same if you search for investment products, and the scammers are paying to get their scam ads right to the top of the search to find people who are actively looking for those products.” Data from the government’s National Anti-Scam Centre show that Australians lost $2.18 billion to scams in 2025, almost 40 per cent — $838 million — of which was from investment scams.
The growth area, according to Young, is targeting people looking for predictable, low-risk investments like term deposits or bonds.
A little knowledge can be a dangerous thing. Older generations understand the value of safe investments, but too many overestimate their knowledge of how to spot scams.
While scammers are going after everyone they can to generate an income, Westpac data shows the demographic most impacted by investment scams is males aged between 51 and 75.
Young says this is not about investors’ greed or naivete. Instead, he says, they are often people who have accumulated wealth over decades and are looking for stability in an uncertain time.
“These scammers are creating entire ecosystems to draw people in, setting up fake comparison sites that lead to fake investment company websites with personalised investment dashboards. In some instances they have fake call centres.” And he says that in an age when AI can generate professional, error-free, comprehensive and entirely fraudulent websites and prospectuses in a matter of minutes, the warning signs are harder to spot.
While a lot of people are aware of the risks of high-yield crypto offers, or other deals with murky reputations, increasingly the bait is term deposits, bonds or commodities like gold or silver.
“Unfortunately we have seen people lose money on things that they don’t think are high risk at all,” says Young.
The offers are attractive but not too attractive, and often the websites are made up to look like real companies with real track records.
The cautious might pause to check the URL, but, as an example, how many would spot the difference, between www.scam-u.com and www.scam-u.com?
In the second, the ‘c’ is from another typeface family: to us there is no appreciable difference, but the computer sees it and directs you into the arms of the scammers.
Young says some scammers even allow their victims to withdraw small initial deposits in order to build confidence before encouraging them to invest more money, although they often impose ‘fees’ for tax clearance, administration fees or verification costs.
Despite the increasing sophistication of scams, Young says there are still some tells that should raise concerns.
“No legitimate investment adviser is going to offer guaranteed low-risk, high-return investments. If someone is creating urgency, telling you to act now, or tying an investment opportunity to current world events, that’s a red flag.” Banks monitor transactions to help stop suspicious transactions but continue to urge people to be on alert.
“We detect most scam payments, but that’s cold comfort for people who have been impacted. This is why we continue to point out the ways scammers are evolving their methods so we can help people avoid them,” says Young.
For people who think they may have been scammed or had their accounts accessed, Westpac has introduced SafeBlock, an emergency security feature that allows customers to instantly lock their bank accounts.
Scams are an ongoing issue in Australia and it has prompted a recent rethink of how they are dealt with, with the government looking to introduce a framework that requires banks, certain digital platforms including social media, and telecommunications providers to take steps to prevent, detect and disrupt scams.
The ecosystem approach is meant to help stop more scams.
However, Young says another area where prevention could be strengthened is the ease of which scammers can create the appearance of a legitimate business.
“It’s incredibly easy to register a fake business and get an ABN, and once these fake businesses look legitimate, they start scamming people,” Young says.
“This is an area we’re keen to work with the government on to shut down.” Beyond this, Young says the most effective defence remains consumer scepticism. “Many of these scams look convincing at first glance,” Young says. “If you’re considering an investment, slow down, do your research and verify every detail independently before parting with your money. “I’d even urge you to have a conversation with a loved one. Sometimes talking it out can help protect you from losing your life savings.”
